text: Article · research post · Connectionism, Thinking Machines Lab's blog · updated 25 November 2026 End-to-End 4-Bit Training Jack Cook, with others at Thinking Machines (Thinking Machines Lab) · published 13 November 2026 In one line: On one model, Inkling 2 Small (594B total, 17B active, a mixture of experts), Thinking Machines ran the expert layers' forward matmuls in NVFP4 and their backward matmuls in MXFP8 re-quantised with stochastic rounding, and sent expert-parallel traffic in 4.5 and 8.25 bits a value; in their largest jobs they report about 8% faster pretraining at about 2% compute efficiency and about 20% faster RL with no discernible difference in reward, both against full MXFP8, with no seeds, loss curves or reward curves published.

text: The idea in one sentence: 4-bit arithmetic is safe where rounding error is random and gets averaged away, and unsafe where it is systematic and compounds, so Thinking Machines put NVFP4 only in the forward matmuls of the expert layers (and the RL sampler, which runs the same forward), kept every backward matmul in MXFP8, and made the hand-over between the two unbiased with stochastic rounding.
